chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Behavioral Economics Is (and Isn't)

lessons.title: Heuristics and Mental Shortcuts: How the Brain Simplifies Economic Choices

children.text: An HR manager in Gurugram screens 200 resumes for one analyst role in under two hours. She cannot deeply evaluate every candidate, so she leans on a fast rule: candidates from certain colleges, with certain certifications listed near the top, "look like" a good analyst, and get shortlisted first. She is satisficing, exactly as Herbert Simon's theory predicts. But how does she actually satisfice, in practice, in the two seconds she spends on each resume? The answer is a heuristic: a specific mental shortcut the brain reaches for automatically. This lesson covers the three shortcuts that show up most often in economic life, at work, at the bank, and at the shop, not just in a stock ticker.

body.text: Bounded rationality explains why people satisfice instead of optimizing. Heuristics are how they actually do it: fast, automatic rules of thumb that substitute a hard question, such as "what are the true odds here," with an easier one, such as "how much does this resemble what I already expect."

children.text: Where Heuristics Come From

markDefs.definition: A simple, automatic mental rule of thumb that produces a fast judgment or decision without requiring a full, careful analysis of all the available information.

children.text: Five years before their more famous 1979 prospect theory paper, Kahneman and Tversky had already published "Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases" in Science in 1974. It named three specific
heuristics

people rely on when judging probability or frequency under uncertainty: representativeness, availability, and anchoring-and-adjustment. Anchoring gets its own full lesson later in this course, once you have seen how businesses deliberately exploit it in pricing. This lesson covers representativeness and availability, plus a third shortcut identified by later researchers: the affect heuristic.
The Representativeness Heuristic: Judging by Resemblance

markDefs.definition: Judging the probability that something belongs to a category by how closely it resembles a typical, stereotypical member of that category, while ignoring how common or rare that category actually is.

children.text: The
representativeness heuristic

means judging probability by resemblance to a mental stereotype rather than by actual statistical likelihood. Consider Ramesh: quiet, precise, wears thick glasses, spends weekends solving crossword puzzles, and studied at a top engineering college. Now ask which is more probable: Ramesh works as a bank probationary officer, or Ramesh works as a bank probationary officer and also plays gully cricket every Sunday.

body.caption: The conjunction rule of probability: two conditions holding together can never be more likely than either condition alone. Adding "plays gully cricket" can only keep the probability the same or lower it, never raise it.

children.text: Most people still pick the second option. It feels more representative of "Ramesh" as a specific, vivid person, even though it describes a strictly smaller, less probable group. Kahneman and Tversky demonstrated this exact pattern in the early 1980s and it became known as the conjunction fallacy: a specific, story-like detail feels more probable than a broader, blander category, even when probability theory guarantees the opposite. The same instinct that makes a resume with a familiar-sounding profile jump out to an HR manager is at work here.

body.title: Spot the conjunction fallacy
body.question: A loan officer meets Meena: she runs a small boutique, dresses sharply, and talks confidently about expanding to a second store. Which statement is more probable?
options: Meena's boutique loan application will be approved
Meena's boutique loan application will be approved and she will also repay ahead of schedule
Both statements are exactly equally probable
There is not enough information to compare the two statements
body.explanation: The first statement alone must be at least as probable as the conjunction of both, by the basic rule of probability. Meena's confident, put-together image makes the more specific, flattering combination feel more likely, which is the representativeness heuristic misleading the loan officer's judgment.

children.text: The Availability Heuristic: Judging by What Comes to Mind Easily

markDefs.definition: Judging how likely or common something is by how easily examples of it come to mind, rather than by its actual statistical frequency. Recent, vivid, or heavily reported events feel more common than they are.

children.text: The
availability heuristic

means judging frequency or risk by how easily examples come to mind, not by the real base rate. Two familiar Indian patterns show this clearly. First, when the RBI places withdrawal restrictions on one urban cooperative bank, a fairly routine and periodic regulatory action affecting a single weak institution, depositors at entirely unrelated, financially healthy cooperative banks nearby sometimes queue up to withdraw their own money too. The news they just watched is far more available in memory than the unremarkable, unreported fact that most banks around them are stable. You will see this exact pattern again, at national scale, in Chapter 6.

Second, sales of Kerala State Lottery tickets and similar state lottery draws typically pick up in the days right after a large jackpot winner is widely reported. The true odds of winning have not moved even slightly, but a vivid, recent, specific winner is far easier to recall than the millions of unreported losing tickets, so the win feels more available, and therefore more likely, than it actually is.

body.text: Availability cuts both ways. It makes rare, vivid risks like a single bank's trouble feel common, and it makes rare, vivid rewards like a lottery win feel reachable. Both errors come from the same shortcut: ease of recall standing in for actual frequency.

children.text: The Affect Heuristic: Judging by Gut Feeling

markDefs.definition: Letting an overall gut feeling, liking or disliking, stand in for a careful, separate evaluation of a specific decision's actual risks and benefits.

children.text: Researcher Paul Slovic and his colleagues named a third shortcut in 2000: the
affect heuristic

. People let a general emotional impression substitute for a careful, separate judgment of risk and benefit. A well-known Indian conglomerate that has earned decades of trust selling steel, salt, and cars carries that same warm feeling into an entirely unrelated financial product it launches. Buyers assume it must be safe and well-run largely because of the brand's overall reputation, without separately checking the specific product's actual terms, fees, or track record. This is the halo effect, the affect heuristic's most common form in consumer finance: a good feeling about the whole company quietly substitutes for scrutiny of the one product actually on offer.

cells: How statistically likely is this, really?
How much does this resemble what I expect?

How frequent or common is this, really?
How easily can I recall an example of this?
Recent, vivid, heavily reported events feel far more common than they are
What are the specific risks and benefits here?
How do I feel about this overall?
A good or bad overall feeling gets applied to a specific decision it has nothing to do with

body.title: Which shortcut is at work?
body.scenario: A hospital's junior doctor sees a patient with chest discomfort. The doctor recently treated two unrelated patients with near-identical symptoms who both turned out to have a serious cardiac condition, a rare diagnosis for someone this patient's age. The doctor immediately orders the full cardiac workup, overriding the far more statistically likely explanation of acid reflux.
body.prompt: Which heuristic is most clearly driving the doctor's decision, and what would correct it?
body.modelAnswer:
1. This is primarily the availability heuristic. The two recent, memorable cardiac cases are easy to recall, which makes a similar-looking case feel far more likely to be cardiac than the actual base rate for this patient's age group justifies.
2. Representativeness may be playing a secondary role too, if the symptoms happen to resemble the doctor's mental picture of "a cardiac case" built from those two recent patients.
3. The correction is not to ignore the doctor's instinct entirely, but to consciously check it against the real base rate for the patient's specific age and risk profile, rather than against how vividly the last two cases are remembered.
4. This is exactly why hospitals use structured diagnostic checklists and clinical scoring systems: they force a comparison against actual statistics instead of recent memory.

body.title: Name the heuristic
body.textWithBlank: Judging how common or risky something is by how easily an example comes to mind, rather than by its real statistical frequency, is called the ___ heuristic.
body.explanation: The availability heuristic explains why a single widely reported event, a bank's trouble or a lottery winner, can distort perceived risk or reward far more than the underlying statistics justify.

body.text: None of these three shortcuts are defects to be trained away entirely. They are fast, low-effort, and right often enough that the brain keeps using them. The danger is not that heuristics exist, it is that businesses and institutions can predict exactly when they will misfire and design around that. Chapter 3 shows precisely how Indian pricing pages do this to anchoring, the third original heuristic, on purpose.

body.title: How many heuristics are there, really?

children.text: Kahneman and Tversky's original 1974 paper named exactly three: representativeness, availability, and anchoring-and-adjustment. Researchers have since proposed many more, including the affect heuristic covered in this lesson, the recognition heuristic, and the fluency heuristic. Not all of them have held up equally well under later replication attempts. What has held up consistently across decades of research is the core claim these three began with: fast judgment relies on shortcuts, and those shortcuts fail in specific, predictable directions rather than randomly.

body.label: The original heuristics paper
body.context: Kahneman and Tversky's "Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases" named representativeness, availability, and anchoring-and-adjustment, five years before their prospect theory paper.

cards.definition: A simple, automatic mental rule of thumb that produces a fast judgment without a full, careful analysis of all available information.
Judging probability by how closely something resembles a typical, stereotypical case, while ignoring how common or rare that category actually is.
The error of judging a specific, story-like combination of two conditions as more probable than either condition alone, which probability theory rules out.
Judging how frequent or risky something is by how easily examples of it come to mind, rather than by its actual statistical frequency.
Letting a general emotional impression, liking or disliking, substitute for a careful, separate evaluation of a specific decision's actual risks and benefits.

points: Heuristics are the specific mental shortcuts people use to satisfice, the fast tools behind the bounded-rationality behavior covered in the previous lesson.
Representativeness judges probability by resemblance to a stereotype, and can make a specific, story-like detail feel more likely than a broader category, even when it logically cannot be.

Availability judges frequency or risk by how easily examples come to mind, which is why one widely reported bank's trouble or one lottery winner distorts perceived risk or reward well beyond the real statistics.
The affect heuristic lets an overall gut feeling about a brand or company substitute for scrutiny of one specific product, the mechanism behind the halo effect in consumer finance.

None of these shortcuts are irrational defects. They are fast and usually accurate, which is exactly why they are predictable enough for pricing pages and institutions to design around, a theme this course returns to from Chapter 3 onward.
